overview.summary: Physiotherapists help people move and function better after injury, illness or surgery, or because of long-term conditions, using exercise, hands-on treatment and advice.
overview.problems: They reduce pain, improve movement and help people return to daily life, work or sport.
overview.worksWith: Patients of all ages, doctors, nurses, occupational therapists and sports coaches.
overview.workplaces: Hospitals, clinics, sports teams, rehabilitation centres, schools, care homes and patients' homes, and some therapists run private practices.

timeline.title: Review patient notes
timeline.description: The physiotherapist reads the notes, goals and progress of the patients booked for the day.
timeline.why: Each treatment builds on what was done before.

timeline.title: Assessing and treating patients
timeline.description: The physiotherapist asks about symptoms, checks movement and strength, explains the findings and starts treatment with exercises or hands-on techniques.
timeline.why: A careful assessment shows what is causing the problem.

timeline.title: Writing notes
timeline.description: The physiotherapist records what was found and what was done.
timeline.why: Records guide later treatment and protect patients.

timeline.title: Exercise sessions and teaching
timeline.description: The physiotherapist guides patients through exercises, adjusts them and teaches patients how to practise at home.
timeline.why: Recovery depends a lot on what patients do between visits.

timeline.title: Teamwork and planning
timeline.description: The physiotherapist talks with doctors, nurses or coaches and updates treatment plans.
timeline.why: Good recovery plans involve everyone who looks after the patient.

timeline.title: Home visits, sports events or ward work
timeline.description: Some physiotherapists travel to patients' homes, work with sports teams or treat patients on hospital wards.
timeline.why: Care is most useful when it happens where the patient needs it.

responsibilities: Referring patients to other professionals when needed
challenges: The work is physically demanding and involves a lot of hands-on handling.
Recovery can be slow, and some patients make limited progress.
Motivating patients to keep exercising is not always easy.
Busy schedules can mean seeing many patients in a day.
Seeing people in pain or with serious conditions can be emotionally tiring.
workEnvironment: Clinics, hospitals, gyms, sports facilities and patients' homes. The work is active, with a lot of standing, moving and hands-on contact. Roles differ from hospital wards to sport settings to private practice.
rewards: Seeing patients regain movement and independence
Working closely with people over time
tradeoffs: Slow or limited progress with some patients
Time pressure when appointment lists are full
Pay that varies by country and setting

activity.title: Learn a gentle stretch and explain it clearly
steps: Choose a simple, gentle stretch from a trusted public health website, such as your national health service.
Read why it is done, how to do it safely and when to stop.
Try it gently yourself, only if you have no pain or injury.
Explain it to a family member in your own words, including when to stop.
Note whether helping someone move better felt rewarding.
activity.outcome: You practise learning how the body moves and explaining an exercise clearly and safely.
activity.safety: Stretch gently and stop if anything hurts. Do not advise or treat anyone who has an injury or pain, because they should see a qualified health professional.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
